newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy Ross prepares for more Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross prepares for more Mideast talks.

text.p: U.S. envoy Dennis Ross planned more talks with Israeli and Palestinian leaders on Tuesday on his mission to mend Middle East peacemaking.
Ross, sent to the region after an Islamic militant suicide bombing, was due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem later in the day, Israeli and U.S. officials said.
PLO officials said the American envoy would also hold a further round of talks in the West Bank town of Ramallah with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
It was not clear when Ross, who began his talks on Sunday, would leave but the State Department said on Monday that he was expected back in Washington within two days.

Ross has sought on his trip, his first since May, to stitch back together Israeli-Palestinian security cooperation following the July 30 attack, which killed 16 people including the two suicide bombers.

A measure of his success will be whether Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, armed with proposals to push final peace talks to a speedy conclusion, decides to make a maiden visit to the region late this month.

"We will take a look at what's happened. We will take a look at what we think we can contribute and on that basis we will have announcements to make about a trip if that's her decision," State Department spokesman James Rubin said in Washington.
Within hours of his arrival on Sunday, Ross brought together Arafat and Israeli officials for the first time since the bombing, which ripped through Jerusalem's main Jewish market.
A second meeting among Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. security officials took place in Ramallah on Monday night.

The fact that the experts were "getting down to the nitty-gritty...(of) what needs to be done is a step in the right direction. But the extent of that progress will be determined by actions, not meetings," Rubin said.

Netanyahu, elected last year on a pledge to keep Israelis safe from the bombers, has accused Arafat of blowing hot and cold on "terrorism", granting Moslem militants opposed to peace moves a haven on territory under Palestinian Authority rule.
The Israeli leader told the U.S. MSNBC network on Monday that security meetings were "meaningless" without action.
"We'd like to see them act against terrorism, stop incitement for violence, collect the bombs...We are looking for results. They have to fight terrorism. Period," he said.
Arafat has insisted he is living up to obligations under interim peace deals and accuses Israel of using the bombing as a pretext to wreck the peace process and weaken his legitimacy.

Netanyahu has clamped a security closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip, imposed economic sanctions on the Palestinian Authority and made a resumption of peace talks conditional on tough moves against militants by Arafat's security forces.
Palestinian officials said Monday night's security meeting had focused on laying down a framework for security coordination but had not tackled what measures the sides should take.
They continued to insist on a linkage between security ties and progress on the political front.
"Any achievement on the security level without equal progress on the political track will be insufficient," Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
Peace talks had already been in crisis over a Jewish settlement Israel began building in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
Palestinians want construction halted, an end to Israel's demolition of Palestinian houses and land confiscations and a lifting of Netanyahu's punitive measures.

In a slight easing of the Israeli clampdown, vegetable trucks from the self-ruled Gaza Strip were allowed into Israel on Tuesday but the closure to tens of thousands of Palestinian workers remained firmly in force.
